content:
North Carolina Republicans went into the Nov. 3 election with a congressional map designed to give them 11 of the state’s 14 seats.

The latest unofficial returns point to an 11–3 split all right – but with Democrats on the 11 side.

That was only one part of what might better be called a blue asteroid than a blue wave. Former Gov. Roy Cooper beat Republican Michael Whatley by nearly 20 points in the US Senate race.

Democratic state Supreme Court Justice Anita Earls won reelection by nearly 18 points.

Democrats won control of the state House for the first time in 16 years and cut the Republican majority in the state Senate to two seats, according to the unofficial returns.

And, in Guilford County, where Democrats already had seven of the nine seats on the Board of Commissioners, voters took care of the other two. Republican Commissioners Alan Perdue and Pat Tillman both lost their reelection bids – setting up Guilford’s first all-Democratic board this century when the new commissioners are sworn in next month.

That’s a real loss of experience and rationality on the board that runs Guilford County.

Together they didn’t have the votes to block the Democrats’ wild spending over the last half decade – but they knew their stuff and asked tough questions in work sessions. Some years they took criticism for voting for a budget shaped by Democrats. But there was a reason to stay in those budget talks. Alston has long pushed for unanimous budget votes, and that gave Perdue and Tillman a chance to get some changes behind the scenes.

Perdue started volunteering at a fire department in Guilford County at 16 and went on to serve as the county’s longtime Emergency Services director. It’s been exactly half a century since he started volunteering, and he’s seen county government from just about every angle – as an employee, a department head, a committee member and a commissioner. He knows Guilford County government inside and out and probably knows more about it than anyone else on the planet.

Tillman, a US Marine Corps combat veteran and current member of the National Guard, raised good questions at meeting and knew the issues very well. And from his years on the Guilford County Board of Education, he knew how the schools operated. When the school system came to the commissioners asking for money, Tillman understood the request from both sides of the table.

It would be hard to find better commissioners than that.

But none of that mattered in an election where voters went to the polls in swarms to angrily vote against Trump. The president’s name wasn’t on the ballot, but Tillman’s and Perdue’s were.

In any normal year, Tillman and Perdue would be back in their seats. As Perdue told the Rhino Times after the election, “There was nothing we could do.”

One Republican state representative told the Rhino Times before the election that he was very afraid the anger at Trump would take down a lot of Republicans, including himself. He ended up losing his race. He said he also thought Whatley was basically insane for making so much of his campaign about helping Trump keep doing what he’d been doing.

“I think he’s going to get his ass handed to him,” the Republican lawmaker told the Rhino before the election – which is exactly what happened.

The Rhino Times also wonders how good a candidate Whatley was. His campaign never even returned calls or emails from the Rhino Times requesting an interview with him. You’d think a candidate for statewide office would want a chance to talk to tens of thousands of readers in Guilford County and beyond – most of whom are conservatives and dedicated voters.

Guilford County Board of Commissioners Chairman Skip Alston had a simple explanation for what happened in the state and in the nation. Trump, he said, had encouraged people to vote as though he were on the ballot.

“And that’s what they did,” Alston said. “They voted them out.”

Alston sees the election as a rebuke of the people in power.

When asked whether North Carolina was now blue or still purple, though, he called it a blue state with a little purple mixed in – a nod to the two-seat Republican edge in the state Senate.

There’s no better place to see how the Republican redistricting strategy came undone than in eastern North Carolina. The 2025 redraw was aimed at Democratic Congressman Don Davis. To make his 1st District more Republican, lawmakers moved six counties out of Republican Congressman Greg Murphy’s neighboring 3rd District and into Davis’ district.

They moved four counties the other way.

Using the 2024 presidential returns, the new lines raised Trump’s share in the 1st District from about 51 percent to 55 percent. That same swap lowered it in the 3rd District from about 60 percent to 56 percent, according to WUNC. The idea was to make Davis easier to beat while leaving Murphy with enough of a cushion.

Davis won anyway.

And in the district Republicans made less safe in their effort to beat Davis, Democrat Raymond Smith pulled ahead after provisional ballots were counted. Murphy, who had declared victory the morning after the election, conceded.

Democrats flipped seats from the Piedmont to the mountains, including the 6th and 9th districts and the 11th District in western North Carolina. And after the county canvass in the 5th District, Democrat Chuck Hubbard led 11-term Republican Congresswoman Virginia Foxx by 331 votes – a margin close enough for Foxx to request a recount.

North Carolina Democratic Party Chair Anderson Clayton discussed the backfire with Tim Miller on The Bulwark podcast. The outlet titled its standalone clip “We Can’t Stop Laughing at the GOP’s Gerrymandering Failure.” Republicans had held 10 of the state’s 14 congressional seats before the redraw. They went looking for one more and are now on track to lose seven.

On the podcast, Clayton told Miller: “I was laughing yesterday, because I was thinking about, wow, if they had left the 2022 map, they would have had four more representatives. Like if we’d had an even fifty-fifty split in North Carolina like we did on free and fair maps, they would still have more representatives right now than they did on the dumbass map that they drew for themselves. I was like, y’all are idiots to be honest with you.”

Texas tried the same thing on a bigger scale.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans there redrew their map to try to pick up five Democratic-held seats. According to The Texas Tribune, they flipped just one of the five and lost two seats that they already held. They were aiming for a 30–8 advantage. They came away with 24 seats, one fewer than they had going in.

For Alston, the question now is what the new balance of power in Raleigh means when Guilford County needs something from the state.

And the county already has something to ask for. On the same ballot that put Democrats in charge of the state House, voters approved a constitutional amendment requiring lawmakers to limit how much local governments can increase their property tax collections. The amendment leaves legislators to decide the size of that limit and what exceptions to allow.

That uncertainty has already reached Guilford’s budget talks. County Manager Victor Isler cited it when he recommended against giving Guilford County Schools the full $5.3 million it requested this month.

Alston said he wants to sit down over breakfast with Guilford’s legislative delegation and show lawmakers the county’s revenue projections and what it expects to spend to serve a growing population. He thinks the new House gives Guilford a better chance of making its case. Republicans will still run the Senate, and Alston said the county may need to find someone on that side willing to listen.

Alston pointed to the school system’s five-year funding plan to explain why the details matter. The Board of Commissioners can project what it would cost to follow that plan, he said, but it still has to figure out what it can afford to promise year after year. He said he doesn’t yet know whether Guilford will need an exception to the cap. That depends on where lawmakers set it.

His more immediate concern is that the outgoing legislature might try to set the limits before the newly elected lawmakers are sworn in.

The new balance of power makes it harder for Republicans to override Democratic Gov. Josh Stein’s vetoes on their own once the new General Assembly takes office. Until then, Alston is watching what the current one might do.
